'expected' must be suggested for full recall; 'acceptable' may be suggested without counting as a false positive. An empty 'expected' is a negative: nothing should be suggested. Labels may name skills another change adds: a name not on disk is dropped, and a case whose expected skills are all missing is skipped. Every skill on disk needs at least one case. The town council voted on Tuesday to close the Harbour Road bridge to cars for eighteen months while its deck is rebuilt. Engineers told the meeting that the steel beneath the roadway has corroded faster than an inspection four years ago predicted, and that patching it again would cost nearly as much as replacing it. Buses will be sent around by the ring road, adding about twelve minutes to the two routes that cross the river, and a footbridge beside the works will stay open to people walking and cycling. Shop owners on the east bank asked for the work to be done in two halves so that one lane could stay open, but the contractor said that would add a year and a third to the cost. The council agreed instead to pay for signs on both approaches, to waive market stall fees on the east bank for the duration, and to review the bus diversion after three months. Two councillors voted against, saying the money should come from the regional transport fund and not from the town's reserves. The finance officer replied that an application to the fund has been made, that an answer is expected in the autumn, and that work cannot wait for it because the weight limit on the bridge would otherwise have to drop below what a fire engine weighs. Work begins in the first week of June. Residents who rely on deliveries across the bridge have been asked to tell the council by the end of the month, so that access can be arranged in the early morning before the crews start. A public drop-in session with the engineers will be held at the library next Thursday evening.

Some background first so this makes sense. My aunt Colette lent me her car for the two weeks I was between jobs in the spring, which was very kind of her, and I told her I would bring it back cleaned and with a full tank. I did fill the tank, but I never got round to having it cleaned, and on the last day I scraped the rear bumper on a bollard in a car park. It is a small mark, but it is there, and I did not mention it when I dropped the keys off because she had guests and it did not feel like the moment. That was three weeks ago. Since then she has rung twice and I let both calls go because I was embarrassed, which I know has made it worse. My mother says Colette has not said anything about the car to her, so she may not have noticed, or she may be waiting for me to bring it up. I have found a body shop near her house that says they can fix a scrape like that in a morning for a fixed price, and I have the money now that I am working again. I would like to own up, apologise for not saying so at the time and for not returning her calls, offer to pay for the repair and a proper valet, and suggest a couple of mornings next week when I could take the car in for her so she does not have to do anything. She does not use messaging apps and she likes things in writing, so it should go to her email address, which is in my contacts under Colette Marchetti. Could you write that to her for me? Warm, not grovelling, no more than three short paragraphs. Let me read it before you send anything.

Can I talk something through with you? Nothing needs doing, I just want another view. My oldest friend and I have known each other since we were nine. Over the last two years she has cancelled on me more often than she has turned up, usually an hour or two before, usually with a reason that is fine by itself: work ran late, her sister needed a lift, she was worn out. Last weekend it was my birthday dinner. I had booked a table for six, and she messaged at five to say she could not make it because she had double-booked with her partner's family. I said it was fine. It was not fine. The thing is, when we do see each other it is as easy as it ever was. She remembers things about my life that nobody else does. When my father was ill she drove four hours to sit with me in a hospital car park. So I do not think she has stopped caring. I think I have slid down her list without her noticing, and I do not know whether saying so would fix it or just make her feel accused. Part of me wants to stop being the one who makes the plans and see what happens. Part of me thinks that is a test she does not know she is taking, which is not fair either. Is there a way to raise it that does not sound like keeping score? And am I being unreasonable to mind this much about a dinner?

I have been writing a poem for my grandmother's ninetieth and I am stuck on which verse to cut, because it runs a little long to read aloud. Here it is.

She kept the garden like a ledger,
every row accounted for,
beans in their columns, peas in their margins,
and weeds shown promptly to the door.

She kept the kitchen like a harbour,
something always coming in,
a neighbour, a nephew, a pan of plums,
the kettle's small insistent din.

She kept her letters in a biscuit tin,
tied up with butcher's string,
and read them on the darker evenings
as other people sing.

She kept her counsel, mostly,
and gave it when we asked,
in sentences as short as stitches
that somehow always last.

She keeps us still, at ninety,
in the orbit of her chair,
each of us a little straighter
for knowing she is there.

Which verse would you drop, and why? I do not want it rewritten, only your opinion on the weakest one.
